sn12.1:1.1: For an overview of this topic, see my Introduction to the Saṁyutta Nikāya.
sn12.1:1.3: In a shift from the previous book, there is no interaction or dialogue; the teaching is a direct address by the Buddha.
sn12.1:1.7: Dependent origination has certain points in common with Vedic cosmogenesis, where the individuation of “name and form” is driven by desire, forged by heat from primordial darkness cloaked in mystery (Rig Veda 3.38, 10.90, 10.121, 10.129). It is deliberately obscured by poets who protect the truth by hiding the highest names (10.5). Such cosmologies were developed in the later stages of the Rig Veda, and further in certain Upaniṣads.
sn12.1:2.1: I give some pre-Buddhist usages to better understand the context. All the terms are from basic Indo-European roots applied in a specific technical sense. In the next discourse we see how the Buddha redefined them to his purpose.
sn12.1:2.2: “Knowledge” (_veda_) was that of the immortal gods, so knowledge itself is immortal, while ignorance (_avijjā_), being perishable, traps the fool in suffering for life after life. Knowledge and ignorance are part of the mortal condition (Atharva Veda 11.8.23). “A man crosses death through ignorance and attains immortality through knowledge” (Īśa Upaniṣad 11; cf. Paiṅgala Upaniṣad 2.11, Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.1, Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.9).
sn12.1:2.3: “Choices” (_saṅkhāra_) fundamentally means to “construct” or “energize” (Sanskrit _samaskurva_, _saṁskāra_). It is used for the “reviving” or “rejuvenation” of the god Pajāpati when he is depleted by the act of creation, like a fire run low or a man after sex (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 7.2.1.5 *et passim*). The sacrificer thereby perpetuates the creative process, building a new self or body (10.4.1.2). The ritual is “performed” by body, speech, and mind in full awareness (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.16.2–3). Thus the creative act became determined by moral “choices”: a person becomes something good by good deeds, bad by bad deeds (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5).
sn12.1:2.4: “Consciousness” (_viññāṇa_, Sanskrit _vijñāna_) means to “know clearly, understand”, and hence the sense of awareness that is conscious of whatever happens. The “self” is the Person made of consciousness (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.16). One who is dying abandons the body and senses, becoming one with consciousness, embraced by previous knowledge and actions (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). They reach out to a new life and become established there, like a caterpillar moving from one leaf to the next.
sn12.1:2.5: “Name” (_nāma_) and “form” (_rūpa_) are the means by which we identify a person of such and such name and appearance (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7). The world manifests as name, form, and action (1.6.1). A virtuous man abandons his old form and fashions a better one as a god, etc. (4.4.4). As the rivers lose their individual names and forms when they enter the ocean, the liberated soul merges with the great Person (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.8, Praśna Upaniṣad 6.5).
sn12.1:2.6: A “field” (_āyatana_) is an “abode” or “proper place” in which one is at rest and safe. Senses are treated unsystematically—the order and number varies, and they are mixed with other things. Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.5.20, for example, says when a man sleeps, he no longer thinks, tastes, smells, sees, or hears. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1 speaks of inadequate (“one-footed”) manifestations of Divinity: speech, breath, eye, ear, mind (_mano_), heart.
sn12.1:2.7: “Contact” (_phassa_, Sanskrit _sparśa_) is literally touch felt by the skin (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.11, 3.2.9). It is poetically extended to touching “heaven” (Rig Veda 2.41.20), “the heart” (4.1.1), or “the truth” (4.50.3). Jains likewise treat contact as physical touch (Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.23), suggesting that its use as a general term for sense contact was a Buddhist innovation.
sn12.1:2.8: “Feeling” (_vedanā_) does not seem to be used in the sense of hedonic experience pre-Buddhist, but we do find it in Jainism (Tattvārtha Sūtra 3.3, 9.32).
sn12.1:2.9: “Craving” (_taṇhā_, Sanskrit _tṛṣṇā_) seems to be always used in the literal sense of “thirst”.
sn12.1:2.10: “Grasping” (_upādāna_) is found widely in later texts in the senses, “take for oneself, appropriate”, and hence to “derive”, as well as “material cause”. But it does not seem to be pre-Buddhist.
sn12.1:2.11: Jains and Hindus know _bhava_ in the sense “course of transmigration”, “ongoing series of births”, but I cannot trace this sense before Buddhism.
sn12.1:2.12: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19 says the unenlightened go “from death to death”.
sn12.1:2.14: There is no corresponding “dependent cessation”. The ending of dependent origination is Nibbana, extinguishment.
sn12.1:3.1: For the general process of dependent origination, compare Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5–7, which says that as a man desires so he wills, as he wills so he acts, and what he acts he attains. He who is attached goes with his deeds to the place he clings. When that deed is exhausted he returns to this world and further deeds. But if he is without desire, desiring only the Self, he attains immortal Divinity.
